content: Mites, along with ticks, are classified under the subclass Acarina (also referred to as Acari) and belong to the class Arachnida. Mites are among the most diverse and ecologically successful groups of invertebrates. They have adapted to an extraordinary variety of habitats, and due to their small size—most being microscopic—they often remain unnoticed. Many mites live freely in soil or water, but a significant number of species exist as parasites on plants or animals, and some even feed on mold. Certain mites are known to be plant pests, such as spider mites (family Tetranychidae), thread-footed mites (family Tarsonemidae), and gall mites (family Eriophyidae). Among the species that parasitize animals are the Sarcoptic Mange mites (family Sarcoptidae), which burrow into the skin, and Demodex mites (family Demodicidae), which inhabit or reside near the hair follicles of mammals, including humans. The house dust mite (family Pyroglyphidae) is perhaps the most well-known mite species. Insects can also host parasitic mites. For example, Varroa destructor attaches to the body of honeybees, while Acarapis woodi (family Tarsonemidae) resides in the tracheae of honeybees. Hundreds of mite species are associated with other bee species, but most of these mites are poorly described and not well understood. Some of these mites are believed to be parasitic, while others may function as beneficial symbionts. To date, over 45,000 species of mites have been described, but scientists estimate that this represents only about 5% of the total diversity of mites. Mites are thought to have existed for approximately 400 million years. The scientific study of mites and ticks is known as acarology. One tropical mite species, Archegozetes longisetosus, is considered one of the strongest animals in the world relative to its body mass (100 μg). It can lift up to 1,182 times its own weight, which is over five times more than what would be expected for such a small organism (Heethoff & Koerner, 2007). Mites are also significant in the context of allergies. They are known to cause various allergic diseases, including hay fever, asthma, and eczema, and they can exacerbate atopic dermatitis. Mites are commonly found in warm and humid environments, such as beds. It is believed that inhalation of mites during sleep exposes the human body to certain antigens, which can eventually trigger hypersensitivity reactions. Dust mite allergens are considered to be among the most potent dust allergens. As with most allergies, the management of mite allergies begins with avoidance. There is substantial evidence supporting the effectiveness of avoidance measures in patients with atopic dermatitis triggered by mite exposure. Regular washing of mattresses and blankets in hot water can help reduce mite exposure. Antihistamines are also beneficial in managing symptoms; for instance, cetirizine has been shown to alleviate allergic symptoms in affected individuals.
